# submission name:

`cpr1_cbq_matched8`

# upload zipped `archive.zip`

[archive.zip](https://github.com/JasonMo123/comma_video_compression_challenge/releases/download/cpr1_cbq_matched8-v1/archive.zip)

SHA-256 `051baf408f57fae3b343d6ee218ab963d070b3935ceb0b2f412c93a53cf3fab0`, 190,212 bytes, single ZIP member `p`.

# report.txt

```yaml
=== Evaluation results over 600 samples ===
  Average PoseNet Distortion: 0.00000896
  Average SegNet Distortion: 0.00029660
  Submission file size: 190,212 bytes
  Original uncompressed size: 37,545,489 bytes
  Compression Rate: 0.00506617
  Final score: 100*segnet_dist + √(10*posenet_dist) + 25*rate = 0.17
```

about 0.16577 

# does your submission require gpu for evaluation (inflation)?

Yes — `linux-nvidia-t4` / CUDA.

# did you include the compression script? and want it to be merged?

No.

# is this submission competitive or innovative? explain why

Competitive, but not innovative. `0.165780` vs `0.172141` for the #130 , measured on the same colab env privately.

It's a tiny tweak on #130, not a new codec. The only thing I changed is the pose carrier: basis atom 2, 5 and 9 drop from 5-bit to 4-bit, then I resolve the existing int12 coefficients against PoseNet with 8 exact full-600 coordinate passes.

# additional comments

I initially wanna try quantization on #130, and I noticed that the env is pretty sensitive in this project, so I try PyTorch MPS and cpu on my computer for pilot testing and Colab T4 for the exact.

At first, I run a small experiment to find out the potential atoms for quantization, atom 9 has least error and then atom 2 and 5 in 4-bit.

| 8-pair screen | Basis bytes saved | Pose MSE |
|---|---:|---:|
| CPR1 baseline | 0 | 2.076384e-5 |
| atom 9 @ 4-bit | 99 | 5.301601e-5 |
| atom 2 @ 4-bit | 163 | 1.513583e-4 |
| atom 5 @ 4-bit | 155 | 1.723275e-4 |

| Scope | CPR1 baseline | atom 9 @ 4-bit without task compensation |
|---|---:|---:|
| 8 pairs | 2.076384e-5 | 5.301601e-5 |
| 100 pairs | 1.843499e-5 | 6.034502e-4 |

However, direct quantization isn’t a good way, I noticed this in a larger scale experiment(about 12x larger). I realize that I have to re-adjust the coefficients.

So the pipeline then becomes like this: quant to 4bits, use jacobian and tune the coefficients, verify with PoseNet, then decide whether this atoms is a candidate or not.

I rollout to full 600 pairs and 2 round tuning for atom 9 showing that the Pose MSE dropped from 2.0409e-5(baseline) to 1.5863e-5(round 2), until here that I prove this method might work! Then is atom 2 and 5, they improved as well. Due to computing resources, I only run experiments for atom 2, 5 and 9.

I fixed atom 2 5 and 9’s 4bits basis and search for better int12 coordinates for all atoms. Still, due to the lack of computing resources, the search isn’t converge, but the result is good enough for now.

additional experiment out of curiosity is: the improvement was caused by the new bit allocation, or mostly by running additional coefficient-search passes? I run a matched control using original CPR1 5bits and my 2 5 9 4bit version. Using same computing time to search new int12 coefficients. Turns out that quantization only lower Pose MSE for 2.55%. Most of the contributions are from searching int12 coefficients.

### Unsuccessful experiments

I started by screening individual atoms at 3-bit and 4-bit precision on a small subset of pairs.

direct quantization alone: looked promising on a small screen, but it broke on larger batches. -> bit allocation and the coefficient values had to be treated together. After changing the basis, I had to re-run coefficient search instead of reusing the old int12 coordinates.

### Lineage

This work builds on CPR1 from #130.

The performance gain comes from re-solving the int12 coefficients under the new basis, not from changing the rest of the codec.

### LLM usage

I used Claude Code with Opus 5 and Codex with 5.6-Sol to inspect the repository and related work, implement and modify the offline experiment scripts, adapt the experiments to PyTorch MPS, prepare Colab/T4 runs, package candidates, and analyze the results. This included the mixed-precision atom screen, Jacobian/Gauss-Newton compensation, exact coordinate search, and the matched control.

The submitted inflater modules are byte-identical to CPR1; the LLM was mainly used for offline experimentation and packaging. But I remain full control of the idea inspiration and where to explore for next step.
